newsitem.title: UK: Accidental MP enters UK parliament.
newsitem.headline: Accidental MP enters UK parliament.

text.p: The man who calls himself "the most accidental member of parliament ever elected" and said standing in Britain's election was more frightening than dodging bullets in Sarajevo begins his parliamentary career on Wednesday.
Veteran BBC war reporter Martin Bell, who became famous for his television reports from Bosnia in his "lucky" white suit, will take his seat as in independent member in a Labour-dominated parliament.

Bell stood as an anti-corruption candidate in the May 1 election against scandal-hit Conservative politician Neil Hamilton. To his surprise Bell was elected, becoming Britain's first independent MP in half a century.
Hamilton has always denied accusations that he accepted money from Mohammed al-Fayed, owner of the luxury Harrods department store, to ask questions in parliament.

But the allegations dogged his election campaign and provoked thousands of voters in his prosperous Tatton constituency in northwest England -- the fifth most secure for the Conservatives --to switch to Bell.
In his diary of the campaign published in the Guardian newspaper, Bell said he was "perhaps the most accidental member of parliament ever elected".

He admitted to being innocent of politics, complained that "Bosnia was surely easier than this", and said he wished he had brought his flak jacket. But he overturned Hamilton's huge majority to win himself a seat in parliament.
Hamilton is now looking for a job. His wife Christine, who had worked as his secretary, is also now unemployed. The couple appealed for work on British radio on Monday.
"We've got to turn our mind to it because we have got a mortgage to pay," Hamilton said. "All contributions will be gratefully received."
The couple also turned up on a television chat show on Tuesday discussing the effects of unemployment on family life.
"It's akin to a bereavement," Hamilton said. "I feel as though I have been bereaved in a sense, because my career is something I have wanted to do since the age of 12 or 13."
After his election defeat Hamilton said he was considering leaving politics for good to take up journalism.
"I've got a number of irons in the fire," Hamilton said. "Journalism, broadcasting is an obvious opportunity. It's the one profession where questions about your integrity don't matter."
